iconic_games_note: Estadio BBVA is a modern (2015) club ground with a substantial football history as the home of C.F. Monterrey: it hosted the second leg of the 2019 CONCACAF Champions League final and the 2021 CONCACAF Champions League final (both Monterrey titles). It also HOSTED — but Monterrey did not win — the 2016 Clausura final (won by Pachuca 2-1 on aggregate; 2nd leg at Estadio BBVA 1-1, att. 50,302) and the 2019 Apertura final vs América (which drew a near-capacity crowd, ~52,929 expected/reported). The 2026 World Cup will be the venue's first men's World Cup matches.

city_history.founded: 1596 (founded 20 September 1596 by Diego de Montemayor as 'Ciudad Metropolitana de Nuestra Señora de Monterrey')
city_history.significance: Capital and largest city of the state of Nuevo León in northeastern Mexico, at the foothills of the Sierra Madre Oriental. It anchors Mexico's second-largest metropolitan area (Monterrey metro pop. ~5.3 million as of 2026; city proper 1,142,194 per the 2020 census) and is the country's leading industrial and business hub — steel, cement, glass, auto parts and brewing — often described as among the wealthiest cities in Latin America. Nicknamed 'La Sultana del Norte'. The Cerro de la Silla ('Saddle Mountain', ~1,820 m) is its defining landmark and is visible from inside Estadio BBVA, whose jagged roofline echoes the mountain's profile.
city_history.football_culture: Monterrey is one of Mexico's most intense football cities, defined by the Clásico Regiomontano derby between C.F. Monterrey (Rayados), who play at Estadio BBVA, and Tigres UANL. Rayados are one of Liga MX's most successful and best-supported clubs and are CONCACAF's most decorated Champions League/Champions Cup side, giving the metro a deep top-flight pedigree even though Estadio BBVA itself only opened in 2015.

stadium_history_facts: Inaugurated on 2 August 2015 (verified vs cited Wikipedia rev.), coinciding with C.F. Monterrey's 70th anniversary; opening match Monterrey 3-0 Benfica (Eusébio Cup).
Construction ran 2011–2015 at a cost of US$200 million (verified vs cited Wikipedia rev.), making it the most expensive stadium in Mexico at the time.
Designed by Populous together with Mexican firm VFO (lead designer Federico Velasco) — verified.
Owned and operated by FEMSA (verified); home of C.F. Monterrey (Rayados), who moved from the 63-year-old Estadio Tecnológico.
First football stadium in North America to earn LEED Silver certification (verified vs cited Wikipedia rev.).

Nicknamed 'El Gigante de Acero' (The Steel Giant) — verified; grandstand inclination of 34 degrees with field-to-seat distance at the FIFA minimum, and the Cerro de la Silla mountain framed by the open northern end.
Hosted the 2019 (second leg) and 2021 CONCACAF Champions League finals, both won by Monterrey (verified vs the two CCL-final Wikipedia articles).
Regular configuration ~53,500 seats: roughly 43,000 general, ~5,000 club seats, and 324 luxury suites (per Goal.com); Wikipedia rev. gives precise 53,529.
